pending_diagnosis: DIAGNOSIS: Fulminant Wilson's Disease (Acute Liver Failure secondary to Wilson Disease presenting with Coombs-negative Hemolytic Anemia) THE SMOKING GUN: An Alkaline Phosphatase to Total Bilirubin ratio of less than 2 (here: 12 / 28.6 = 0.42) paired with an AST:ALT ratio greater than 2.2 in a young patient with Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the ATP7B gene, which impairs biliary copper excretion and systemic copper incorporation into ceruloplasmin. Over years, copper accumulates silently in hepatic parenchymal tissue. In fulminant presentations, massive hepatocyte necrosis triggers a sudden, catastrophic dumping of ionic free copper into the systemic circulation. This circulating copper causes direct oxidative damage to erythrocyte membranes, precipitating severe Coombs-negative intravascular hemolysis, while simultaneously depositing in the renal tubules to produce acute renal failure. Crucially, free ionic copper competes with and displaces zinc, an essential cofactor, at the active site of the alkaline phosphatase metalloenzyme, paradoxically inactivating it and producing an abnormally suppressed ALP level despite profound hyperbilirubinemia.
